name: Omar Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Omar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. First, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Omar, 27. I work for Thornbury Agri, a big farming company with 2,500 acres of wheat, oilseed rape and beans, and a beef finishing unit with about 600 cattle. I've been there three years and I'm still one of the juniors. My wife Ayesha and I got married last spring, and we live in a rented house in the village. With my dad's help I bought 20 acres of grazing two years ago, which I rent to a neighbour, and we've got over a year of savings because one day I want my own farm.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In the growing season I'm on a tractor most days, drilling or rolling or carting, with GPS steering doing most of the straight lines. In winter I'm in the beef unit, feeding, bedding and moving cattle. I'm still learning things like setting up the sprayer and reading the yield maps, and the senior drivers know it. I like a good long day drilling when the soil's right. What wears me out is the company's rules, a form for everything, and managers who've never been in a cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's get back to real work. Farming's about soil, weather and hard graft, not chatbots. I'd say it to the lads in the canteen and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved. My plan is to save, learn, and one day farm my own land. If nothing changes, that plan still works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Thornbury, learn the sprayer and the yield maps properly. Keep saving, maybe buy another 10 acres if it comes up. Keep renting my field to Mr Hughes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use GPS steering already. Do you use AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I asked one to explain a soil test once, and it was decent. The GPS I use every day, but that's been around for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does this picture mean for your plan to have your own farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes, which is good. Another five or six years of saving and learning, then I start looking at a small farm to rent, with my 20 acres as a base. My dad did it that way with his shop.

S0.say: He'd say good, let's get back to real work, because farming is about soil, weather and hard graft. He'd say it in the canteen and leave it there.
S0.think: Privately he'd be relieved, because his plan to save, learn and one day farm his own land still works.
S0.do: Keeps going at the company, learns the sprayer and yield maps, and keeps saving. Looks at buying another 10 acres if it comes up and keeps renting out his field.
S0.quote: My plan is to save, learn, and one day farm my own land.
S0.fieldNote: Omar is driven by one clear goal: owning a farm. He's comfortable with proven tech like GPS steering but cautious about anything new. His father's shop is his model of how to build something step by step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market will sort it out. Some jobs go, new ones come, and people who work hard will be fine. I'd say young farmers should learn the new kit and stop waiting for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit nervous. Thornbury cuts staff the minute it saves a penny. I'm junior, so I'd be one of the first in line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new tools once the senior drivers were using them, so I'm not the one left behind. I'd keep saving harder, because my own farm is the safest job I'll ever have. And I'd look at buying the next field if it came up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thornbury is a big company. How would they handle it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quickly and coldly. They'd bring in the autonomous tractors as soon as the numbers worked, and the head office would decide, not the farm manager. Three or four of us would be gone in a season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the machines. The company, maybe, for not caring about the people. And the government, for making it so expensive to start a small farm that everyone has to work for a company like Thornbury.

S1.say: He'd say the market will sort it out, and people who work hard will be fine. Young farmers should learn the new kit and stop waiting for help.
S1.think: Privately he's a bit nervous, because the company cuts staff the moment it saves money. As a junior he'd be among the first to go.
S1.do: Learns the new tools once the senior drivers use them and saves harder towards his own farm. Looks at buying the next field if it comes up.
S1.feel: Uneasy and watchful, not losing sleep.
S1.quote: My own farm is the safest job I'll ever have.
S1.fieldNote: His public line is free-market confidence, but privately he sees his employer as cold and himself as first in line. He blames the cost of starting a small farm more than the machines. His answer to risk is owning land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast, but I wouldn't say the government should stop it. I'd say people need to be ready to work for themselves. Families need to look after their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means my job at Thornbury is gone, probably within a year. And my plan, save for ten years and then farm, doesn't work any more. That's what hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything we don't need straight away. I'd talk to my dad about buying more land quickly, while prices are still normal, maybe borrowing from the family. And I'd look at whether I could farm my own 20 acres with hired robots instead of renting them out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My plan's knocked over, but I've still got something to stand on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your 20 acres and your savings. What do they do for you in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They keep me standing. Land doesn't disappear. If robots do the work, the person who owns the field still owns the harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Ayesha talk about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After evening prayers, in the kitchen. Ayesha's an accountant at the dentist's, so her job might go too. She'd say we're lucky, and she'd be right, but I'd be lying awake doing sums.

S2.say: He'd say it's going too fast but wouldn't call on the government to stop it. People need to be ready to work for themselves, and families need to look after their own.
S2.think: Privately he thinks his job is gone within a year and his ten-year plan to farm doesn't work any more. That's what hurts most.
S2.do: Cuts non-essential spending straight away and talks to his father about buying more land quickly with family help. Looks at farming his own 20 acres with hired robots instead of renting them out.
S2.feel: Anxious, with his plan knocked over but something solid to stand on.
S2.quote: If robots do the work, the person who owns the field still owns the harvest.
S2.fieldNote: His land and savings keep him out of alarm, and he sees land as the one thing that holds value. His public line refuses to ask for government help, in line with his outlook. The loss of a long, careful plan hurts him more than the job itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for anyone willing to work to get ready. I'd tell young farmers to buy land or learn a trade now. I'd say it at the young farmers' club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years could actually work for me. I'd buy more land and get the robots once they're proven, and farm it myself. By 2031 I'd be a small farmer, not a company driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd buy another 10 or 20 acres with savings and a family loan. I'd learn the AI tools and autonomous tractors at Thornbury, on their time. I'd stop renting my field out and start farming it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different with five years compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a rush. Five is a plan. With five years I can learn on the company's machines and buy my own once the prices drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Thornbury?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not straight away. They're paying me to learn exactly what I need. I'd leave when my own land could pay us.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough for anyone willing to work to get ready. Young farmers should buy land or learn a trade now.
S3.think: Privately he thinks five years could work for him: buy land, get robots once proven, and farm it himself. By 2031 he'd be a small farmer, not a company driver.
S3.do: Buys another 10 to 20 acres in the first year with savings and a family loan. Learns AI tools and autonomous tractors at his job and starts farming his own field instead of renting it out.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more hopeful than in the fast version.
S3.quote: Two years is a rush. Five is a plan.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time revives his life plan, just faster. He'd use his employer's machines to learn before buying his own, which is typical of his steady approach. His outlook comes through in praising those willing to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who works hard and plans can come out fine. I'd say the government should keep out of the way and make it easier to buy land. That's my line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one suits me. It's almost exactly my plan. By 2036 I want to own my farm and run it with the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Thornbury for now, keep saving, and buy land when it comes up. Learn the autonomous kit as Thornbury brings it in. Around 2030 I'd start farming my own land full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's close to what I'd already planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is close to your original plan. Does that make it easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it's my plan with a deadline. My dad says a plan without a deadline is a wish. Now I've got one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change anything about family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have children in a few years, as we planned. I'd want them to grow up on our own land. That's the point of all of it.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who works hard and plans can come out fine. The government should keep out of the way and make land easier to buy.
S4.think: Privately this one suits him, because it's almost exactly his plan. By 2036 he wants to own a farm and run it with the machines.
S4.do: Keeps working at the company, keeps saving and buys land when it comes up. Learns the autonomous machinery as it arrives and aims to farm his own land full time around 2030.
S4.feel: Calm, because it's close to what he'd already planned.
S4.quote: My dad says a plan without a deadline is a wish. Now I've got one.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years matches his own timeline, so the scenario feels like confirmation rather than threat. He's comfortable with machines as long as he owns them. Children growing up on their own land is the point of all his plans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it knocks my plan over before I've got enough land. What would help is making land easier to buy for young farmers, and less red tape, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who owns the land. Everyone asks who'll lose their job. The bigger question is who owns the fields when the robots are doing the work.

headlineQuote: The bigger question is who owns the fields when the robots are doing the work.
portrait: Omar Patel is a 27-year-old junior tractor driver and stockman at Thornbury Agri, a large farming company with arable land and a beef unit. He's newly married to Ayesha, owns 20 acres he bought with his father's help, and has more than a year's savings towards a farm of his own. He's traditional and free-market, uses proven tech like GPS steering and AI now and then, and sees land ownership as the safest job there is. The two-year AGI picture makes him anxious because it wrecks his long plan, but with five or ten years he'd buy land, learn the machines on the company's time and farm for himself.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it knocks over his plan before he has enough land.
whatWouldHelp: Making land easier for young farmers to buy, with less red tape, rather than handouts.
